q: A manufactured article is ready in a shop for despatch to the stores depot for stocking. Before it can be taken into stores stock, the article must first be:

options.A: Inspected and accepted as conforming to the prescribed specifications
options.B: Paid for by the stores depot in advance
options.C: Entered in the Plant Register of the workshop
options.D: Approved by the Railway Board for transfer

e: A manufactured article ready for despatch to stores must first be inspected and accepted as conforming to the prescribed specifications before it can be taken into stores stock.

q: Which of the following best brings out the nature of Periodic Overhaul, as distinct from ordinary repairs of a rolling stock unit?

options.A: The unit is merely washed and examined before being returned to service
options.B: The unit is completely dismantled, examined and renewed or repaired so as to restore it to the prescribed standard
options.C: Only the part reported defective is attended to
options.D: The unit is repaired without being taken out of service

e: Periodic Overhaul is distinct from ordinary repairs because the unit is completely dismantled, examined and renewed or repaired so as to restore it to the prescribed standard.

q: In the programme terminology of a workshop, the term 'arisings' refers to:

options.A: The scrap arising from jobs in the shops during a period
options.B: The new machines arising for installation under the Machinery and Plant Programme
options.C: The rolling stock becoming due for Periodic Overhaul during a period
options.D: The staff arising for promotion in the workshop during a period

e: In workshop programme terminology, arisings means the rolling stock becoming due for Periodic Overhaul during a period, on the basis of which the overhaul programme is framed.

q: A rolling stock unit is said to be 'homed' to a particular workshop, which means that the workshop:

options.A: Manufactured the unit originally
options.B: Stores the unit when it is not in use
options.C: Pays the wages of the crew of the unit
options.D: Is responsible for carrying out the Periodic Overhaul of that unit

e: A rolling stock unit is homed to the workshop that is responsible for carrying out its Periodic Overhaul, irrespective of where the unit normally works.

q: A Government department asks a workshop to execute a work for it on a deposit-work basis. Before the work is taken in hand, the department is required to:

options.A: Deposit the estimated cost of the work, together with departmental charges, in advance with the Railway
options.B: Execute a bank guarantee for double the estimated cost of the work
options.C: Obtain a special work order from the Railway Board for the work
options.D: Pay only after the work is completed and the bill is raised

e: Work done for a Government department on a deposit-work basis is taken in hand only after the department deposits the estimated cost, together with departmental charges, in advance with the Railway.

q: A private party approaches a railway workshop for the execution of a job for his own use. Such work may be undertaken by the workshop:

options.A: In no circumstances at all
options.B: Free of charge, as a public service
options.C: Only with the sanction of the competent authority, the full cost together with departmental charges being recovered from the party
options.D: On recovery of the cost of material used on the work only

e: Work for a private party may be undertaken by a workshop only with the sanction of the competent authority, the full cost together with departmental charges being recovered from the party.

q: Departmental charges levied in addition to cost on work done by a workshop for other departments or outside bodies represent broadly:

options.A: A profit margin retained by the Railway Board
options.B: A recovery towards the establishment, supervision and tools and plant expenses of the department executing the work
options.C: The cost of the raw material used on the work
options.D: A penalty imposed on the indenting department for placing the work

e: Departmental charges levied over cost on work for other departments or outside bodies recover broadly the establishment, supervision and tools and plant expenses of the executing department.

q: The statement which shows, shop-wise, both the outturn turned out and the outlay incurred by the shops of a workshop is compiled at intervals of:

options.A: Five years
options.B: Audit inspections only
options.C: One year, along with the annual accounts
options.D: Every month

e: The statement showing shop-wise both the outturn turned out and the outlay incurred by the shops of a workshop is compiled every month.

q: Internal check of labour pay sheets and stores issues and compilation of the cost of jobs in a workshop is the responsibility of:

options.A: The Workshop Accounts Office
options.B: The Production Control Organisation
options.C: The stores depot attached to the workshop
options.D: The office of the Chief Workshop Manager

e: Internal check of labour pay sheets and stores issues and compilation of the cost of jobs in a workshop is the responsibility of the Workshop Accounts Office.

q: The detailed job-cost record in the form of the Workshop General Register is kept and maintained by:

options.A: The stores depot attached to the workshop
options.B: The Workshop Accounts Office
options.C: The Production Control Organisation of the workshop
options.D: The office of the Chief Workshop Manager

e: The detailed job-cost record in the form of the Workshop General Register is kept and maintained by the Workshop Accounts Office.

q: Which of the following correctly characterises the budget framed under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense in a workshop?

options.A: It is a final Demand for Grants of the workshop
options.B: It is a part of the Stores Budget of the railway
options.C: It is an outlay (suspense) budget, the expenditure finding final allocation under Capital, Revenue or Stores heads on transfer of the outturn
options.D: It is a budget of the earnings expected from the outturn of the workshop

e: The Workshop Manufacturing Suspense budget is an outlay or suspense budget, the expenditure finding final allocation under Capital, Revenue or Stores heads when the outturn is transferred out.

q: During the execution of a workshop job it is found that its cost will exceed the sanctioned estimate. The excess expenditure on the job may be incurred only after:

options.A: Sanction of a revised estimate by the competent authority
options.B: A verbal approval of the shop incharge is obtained
options.C: The excess is adjusted against savings on some other job, without any sanction
options.D: The close of the financial year, when the accounts are finalised

e: If a job's cost will exceed the sanctioned estimate, the excess expenditure may be incurred only after sanction of a revised estimate by the competent authority.

q: The cost of rectifying articles rejected on account of bad workmanship in a workshop is accounted for as:

options.A: A normal addition to the cost of the original job on which the articles were produced
options.B: Cost of defective work charged to shop on-cost, so that the legitimate cost of the job is not inflated
options.C: A recovery from the Provident Fund of the worker concerned
options.D: Capital expenditure of the workshop

e: Cost of rectifying articles rejected for bad workmanship is charged as cost of defective work to shop on-cost, so that the legitimate cost of the job is not inflated by the fault.

q: Rejection of articles in a workshop beyond the normal process limits is treated, for the purpose of costing the good output, in the manner that:

options.A: Its entire cost is loaded on the cost of the good output of the period
options.B: Its cost is recovered from the stores depot which supplied the material
options.C: Its cost is added to the cost of the next batch taken up in the shop
options.D: Its cost, less the scrap value realised, is treated as a loss or on-cost item and is not loaded on good production

e: Cost of rejections beyond normal process limits, less scrap value realised, is treated as a loss or on-cost item and is not loaded on the cost of good production.

q: Foundry costing in a workshop is generally expressed in terms of:

options.A: Cost per casting, irrespective of its size or weight
options.B: Cost per moulding box used in the foundry
options.C: Cost per unit weight of good castings produced
options.D: Cost per worker employed in the foundry

e: Foundry costing is generally expressed as cost per unit weight of good castings produced, since castings differ in size and weight and weight is the common measure.

q: Melting loss of metal by oxidation and the like, during melting in a foundry furnace, has the effect of:

options.A: Increasing the metal cost that has to be borne by the good castings produced
options.B: Reducing the cost of the castings produced in the foundry
options.C: Being recovered in full as scrap from the furnace
options.D: Being charged to the pattern shop as its on-cost

e: Melting loss by oxidation and the like is metal lost in melting, so the cost of metal charged must be borne by the good castings produced, increasing their metal cost.

q: A job under execution passes from one shop to another within the same workshop for a further operation. In such a case:

options.A: The work order is closed in the first shop and a fresh work order is opened in the next shop
options.B: The job remains under the same work order and continues under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense until its final completion
options.C: The cost accumulated up to that stage is transferred out to the final head of account
options.D: The job is treated as completed at the end of the operation in each shop

e: When a job passes from one shop to another in the same workshop for a further operation, it remains under the same work order and under Workshop Manufacturing Suspense until final completion.

q: At the periodical review of Workshop Manufacturing Suspense, the age analysis of the outstanding balance classifies the jobs according to:

options.A: The trade of the workers employed on the jobs
options.B: The type of material consumed on the jobs
options.C: The names of the shop incharges concerned
options.D: The period for which each job or work order has remained open

e: At the periodical review of Workshop Manufacturing Suspense, age analysis classifies outstanding jobs according to the period for which each job or work order has remained open.

q: A work order against which no expenditure has been booked for a long period is lying dormant. At the review of Workshop Manufacturing Suspense, such a work order is dealt with by:

options.A: Automatically writing off its balance to revenue
options.B: Transferring its balance to the oldest running job of the shop
options.C: Calling for the reasons for the stoppage, and either expediting its completion or closing it under competent orders
options.D: Omitting it from all future reviews of the suspense head

e: A dormant work order with no booking for long is dealt with at the review by calling for the reasons for stoppage, and either expediting completion or closing it under competent orders.

q: The Workshop Accounts Office receives a copy of every work order issued in a workshop. This enables it to:

options.A: Watch the charges booked against the work order and compile the cost of the job in the Workshop General Register
options.B: Fix the wages of the staff who will work on the job
options.C: Purchase the material required for the job
options.D: Sell the finished articles produced on the job

e: A copy of every work order is received by the Workshop Accounts Office, enabling it to watch charges booked against the order and compile the job's cost in the Workshop General Register.

q: Labour pay sheets in a workshop are drawn up on the basis of the time and tally sheets rendered by the shops. The office which prepares these pay sheets is:

options.A: The Personnel Branch, from the leave records of the staff
options.B: The Accounts office
options.C: The Cash office, from the attendance register of the workshop
options.D: The Production Control Organisation, from the route cards

e: Labour pay sheets are prepared by the Accounts office on the basis of the time and tally sheets rendered by the shops showing time booked on jobs.

q: A completion report prepared on the completion of a workshop job serves to:

options.A: Fix the pay of the staff who worked on the job
options.B: Close the accounts of the workshop for the month
options.C: Revise the stores price ledger of the depot
options.D: Record the final cost of the job and compare it with the sanctioned estimate

e: A completion report on a finished job records the final cost of the job and compares it with the sanctioned estimate, so excess or savings can be seen and explained.

q: Incentive bonus earned by a workshop worker under the incentive scheme is:

options.A: Paid in cash on the day each job is completed by him
options.B: Credited to the Provident Fund account of the worker
options.C: Computed on the jobs completed during the month and paid along with the monthly wages
options.D: Paid annually along with the Productivity Linked Bonus

e: Incentive bonus is computed on the jobs completed during the month on the basis of allowed and taken time, and is paid along with the monthly wages of the worker.

q: For fixing the target outturn of a group under the Group Incentive Scheme, the two factors mainly taken into account are:

options.A: The sanctioned strength of the group and the allowed-time norms for the units to be turned out
options.B: The total earnings of the workshop in the previous year and the number of machines installed
options.C: The number of machines installed in the shop and the floor area of the shop
options.D: The outturn of the best-performing group of the workshop in the previous year

e: Target outturn of a group under the Group Incentive Scheme is fixed mainly with reference to the sanctioned strength of the group and the allowed-time norms for the units to be turned out.

q: A standing work order in a workshop can be recognised by the feature that:

options.A: A fresh number is allotted to it on every occasion on which the work is done
options.B: Its number is allotted by the Railway Board for each item of work
options.C: It is identified only by the name of the shop, without any number
options.D: It bears a fixed number allotted to a specified class of routine and repetitive work, against which charges are booked as and when such work is done

e: A standing work order bears a fixed number allotted to a specified class of routine and repetitive work, against which charges are booked as and when such work is done.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, effective and suitable provision is required to be made in every factory for securing and maintaining, in every workroom:

options.A: Air-conditioning at a fixed temperature throughout the year
options.B: Adequate ventilation by the circulation of fresh air, and such a temperature as will secure reasonable conditions of comfort and prevent injury to health
options.C: Ventilation only in workrooms where dust or fume is generated
options.D: Windows opening directly to the open air in every workroom, in place of all other ventilation

e: Section 13 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires adequate ventilation by circulation of fresh air and a temperature securing reasonable comfort and preventing injury to health in every workroom.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, where a manufacturing process carried on in a factory produces dust or fume of such a nature as is likely to be injurious or offensive to the workers, the effective measures required to prevent its inhalation and accumulation include:

options.A: Issue of cloth masks to the workers as the only measure
options.B: Dispersal of the dust by fans into the general air of the workroom
options.C: Periodic sweeping of the workroom after the close of work
options.D: Application of an exhaust appliance as near as possible to the point of origin of the dust or fume, so as to prevent its accumulation in the workroom

e: Section 14 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires an exhaust appliance applied as near as possible to the point of origin of injurious dust or fume, to prevent its inhalation and accumulation.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, where the humidity of the air in a factory is artificially increased, the requirement regarding the water used for the purpose is that:

options.A: It shall be taken from a source of public water supply or other source of drinking water, or be effectively purified before use
options.B: It may be taken from any well or tank in the factory without purification
options.C: It shall be the water condensed from the steam pipes of the factory
options.D: No condition is prescribed for the water so used

e: Section 15 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires water used for artificially increasing humidity to be taken from a drinking water source or effectively purified before use.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, in computing the cubic space available for each worker in a workroom for the purposes of the provision against overcrowding:

options.A: The whole height of the room, however high, is taken into account
options.B: Space below the level of the floor is also counted
options.C: No account is taken of any space more than 4.2 metres above the level of the floor of the workroom
options.D: The space occupied by machines is added to the space available for workers

e: Section 16 of the Factories Act, 1948 provides that in computing cubic space per worker for overcrowding, no account is taken of space more than 4.2 metres above the floor level.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, every factory is required to provide, for the use of workers:

options.A: Latrines for male workers only, urinals being provided only in factories with more than 500 workers
options.B: Sufficient latrine and urinal accommodation of prescribed types, conveniently situated and accessible to workers at all times while they are at the factory, with separate enclosed accommodation for male and female workers
options.C: Latrines and urinals which remain locked during working hours
options.D: A single common latrine for all workers, irrespective of sex

e: Section 19 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires sufficient latrine and urinal accommodation of prescribed types, conveniently situated and accessible at all times, with separate enclosed accommodation for male and female workers.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, where any part of the plant used in a manufacturing process is operated at a pressure above atmospheric pressure, it is required that:

options.A: The plant be operated at the highest pressure it can withstand
options.B: The pressure be recorded only once a year
options.C: No examination of the plant is necessary so long as it is in working order
options.D: Effective measures shall be taken to ensure that the safe working pressure of that part of the plant is not exceeded

e: Section 31 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires effective measures to ensure that the safe working pressure of plant operated above atmospheric pressure is not exceeded.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, every fixed vessel, structure, sump or pit in a factory which, by reason of its depth, position or construction, is or may be a source of danger, and every opening in a floor, is required to be:

options.A: Securely covered or securely fenced
options.B: Merely marked with a painted warning line
options.C: Filled with water up to the brim
options.D: Left open but watched by a worker posted at the spot

e: Section 33 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires every fixed vessel, sump, pit or floor opening that may be a source of danger to be securely covered or securely fenced.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, the provision relating to the lifting and carrying of heavy loads in a factory is that:

options.A: A worker may be required to lift any load if he is paid overtime for it
options.B: The maximum load is fixed by the occupier of each factory at his discretion
options.C: No worker shall be employed to lift, carry or move any load so heavy as to be likely to cause him injury
options.D: Heavy loads may be carried by young persons under supervision

e: Section 34 of the Factories Act, 1948 provides that no worker shall be employed to lift, carry or move any load so heavy as to be likely to cause him injury.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, for the protection of the eyes of persons employed on or in the immediate vicinity of a process which may cause injury to the eyes from particles or fragments thrown off, or from exposure to excessive light, the requirement is that:

options.A: The workers be advised to look away from the process while working
options.B: The process be carried on only during night hours
options.C: Dark glasses be purchased by the workers at their own cost
options.D: Effective screens or suitable goggles shall be provided for the protection of the persons employed

e: Section 35 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires effective screens or suitable goggles to be provided to protect the eyes of persons employed on or near a process that may injure the eyes.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, where a manufacturing process produces dust, gas, fume or vapour of such a nature and to such an extent as is liable to explode on ignition, the measures required to be taken include:

options.A: Leaving the plant open so that the dust escapes freely into the air
options.B: All practicable measures to prevent any explosion, by effective enclosure of the plant used in the process, removal or prevention of accumulation of the dust or fume, and exclusion or effective enclosure of all possible sources of ignition
options.C: Prohibiting the use of electricity anywhere in the factory
options.D: Wetting the floor of the workroom once a week

e: Section 36A of the Factories Act, 1948 requires all practicable measures against explosion of inflammable dust or gas, by enclosure of plant, removal of accumulations and exclusion or enclosure of ignition sources.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, with reference to precautions in case of fire in a factory, it is required that:

options.A: The doors affording exit from any room shall not be locked or fastened so that they cannot be easily and immediately opened from the inside, and means of escape in case of fire shall be provided and maintained
options.B: All exits be kept locked from outside during working hours to prevent workers leaving
options.C: Fire escapes be provided only in factories employing more than 1,000 workers
options.D: The workers be allowed to use the goods lifts as the sole means of escape

e: Section 38 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires means of escape in case of fire to be provided and maintained, and exit doors not to be locked or fastened so they cannot be easily and immediately opened from inside.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, the examination of machinery in motion, and the lubrication or adjustment of parts while the machinery is in motion, where necessary, shall be carried out:

options.A: By any worker available in the shop at the time
options.B: By a young person under the supervision of the chargeman
options.C: Only by a specially trained adult male worker wearing tight-fitting clothing provided by the occupier, whose name is recorded in the prescribed register
options.D: By the worker who happens to operate the machine, whether trained or not

e: Section 22 of the Factories Act, 1948 permits examination or lubrication of machinery in motion only by a specially trained adult male worker in tight-fitting clothing provided by the occupier, whose name is recorded in the prescribed register.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, in every factory there shall be provided and maintained:

options.A: A reserve engine to take over the work in case of breakdown
options.B: Duplicate transmission machinery for every machine
options.C: A siren to be sounded at the start and close of work
options.D: Suitable devices for cutting off power in emergencies from any room, which shall not be locked up or obstructed in a manner that prevents their immediate use

e: Section 24 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires suitable devices for cutting off power in emergencies from any room, which shall not be locked up or obstructed so as to prevent their immediate use.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, in respect of revolving machinery in a factory, such as a grindstone or abrasive wheel or a revolving vessel, it is required that:

options.A: The speed of revolution may be fixed by the operator of the machine
options.B: A notice indicating the maximum safe working peripheral speed of the revolving part shall be affixed on or in the immediate vicinity of the machine, and that speed shall not be exceeded
options.C: No notice of speed is required, the machine being run by its sound
options.D: The revolving part be tested once at the time of installation and never thereafter

e: Section 25 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires a notice of the maximum safe working peripheral speed to be affixed on or near revolving machinery such as a grindstone, and that speed shall not be exceeded.

q:
Consider the following statements about the general duties of the occupier of a factory under the Factories Act, 1948:
1. Every occupier shall ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare of all workers while they are at work in the factory.
2. These duties extend to the provision and maintenance of plant and systems of work that are, so far as is reasonably practicable, safe and without risks to health.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: Both 1 and 2
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Section 7A of the Factories Act, 1948 casts on the occupier the duty to ensure, so far as reasonably practicable, workers' health, safety and welfare, including safe plant and systems of work. Hence both.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, where a worker in a factory works in a shift which extends beyond midnight:

options.A: He is not entitled to any weekly holiday for that week
options.B: His holiday for the week is reckoned as twelve hours only
options.C: A holiday for a whole day for him means a period of twenty-four consecutive hours beginning when his shift ends
options.D: He must be given two consecutive days off in the following week in all cases

e: Section 52 of the Factories Act, 1948 provides that for a worker whose shift extends beyond midnight, a holiday for a whole day means twenty-four consecutive hours beginning when his shift ends.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, the register of adult workers maintained for a factory:

options.A: Shall be maintained by the manager of the factory and shall be available for inspection by the Inspector at all times during working hours, or when any work is being carried on in the factory
options.B: Is kept by the workers' union of the factory
options.C: Is maintained only in factories employing more than 500 workers
options.D: Need be produced before an Inspector only once in five years

e: Section 62 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires the register of adult workers to be maintained by the manager and available for inspection by the Inspector at all times during working hours.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, a young person shall not be required or allowed to work in any factory unless:

options.A: He has completed eighteen years of age
options.B: He is accompanied by an adult worker throughout the shift
options.C: The manager of the factory has given him a written permission
options.D: A certificate of fitness for such work, granted to him by a certifying surgeon, is in the custody of the manager of the factory, and he carries, while he is at work, a token giving a reference to the certificate

e: Section 67 read with Section 68 of the Factories Act, 1948 bars a young person from working unless a certifying surgeon's certificate of fitness is in the manager's custody and he carries a token referring to it.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, an adolescent who has been granted a certificate of fitness to work in a factory and is carrying a token giving a reference to the certificate is:

options.A: Treated as a child for all purposes of the Act
options.B: Deemed to be an adult for all the purposes of the provisions relating to hours of work of adult workers and to annual leave with wages
options.C: Permitted to work only during night hours
options.D: Entitled to work without any restriction of hours

e: Section 70 of the Factories Act, 1948 deems an adolescent holding a certificate of fitness and carrying the token to be an adult for the provisions on hours of work of adults and annual leave with wages.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, the period of work of a child who is allowed to work in a factory is limited so that:

options.A: It does not exceed six hours in any day
options.B: It does not exceed five hours in any day
options.C: It does not exceed four and a half hours in any day, and the child is not employed during the night
options.D: It does not exceed eight hours in any day

e: Section 71 of the Factories Act, 1948 limits a child's work to four and a half hours in any day and prohibits employment of a child during the night.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, in respect of the employment of women in a factory, the restriction is that:

options.A: No woman shall be required or allowed to work in any factory except between the hours of 6 a.m. and 7 p.m., and any variation of these limits by the State Government shall not authorise the employment of a woman between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m.
options.B: A woman may be employed at any hour of the day or night without restriction
options.C: A woman shall not be employed in a factory in any circumstances
options.D: A woman may be employed between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. with the permission of the manager alone

e: Section 66 of the Factories Act, 1948 restricts women's work to between 6 a.m. and 7 p.m., and no State variation may authorise employment of a woman between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, where a medical practitioner attends on a person in a factory whom he believes to be suffering from any disease specified in the Third Schedule of the Act, he is required to:

options.A: Inform only the family of the worker concerned
options.B: Report the matter to the workers' union of the factory
options.C: Treat the worker and keep the matter confidential in all cases
options.D: Forthwith send a report to the office of the Chief Inspector of Factories, stating the name and address of the patient, the disease and the name and address of the factory in which the patient is employed

e: Section 89 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires a medical practitioner attending a factory person believed to suffer from a Third Schedule disease to forthwith report it to the Chief Inspector's office with the prescribed particulars.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, operations in a factory which are declared to be dangerous operations are dealt with in that:

options.A: The occupier alone decides the safeguards for such operations
options.B: The State Government may make rules declaring an operation to be dangerous and prohibiting or regulating the employment of women, adolescents or children in such an operation
options.C: Such operations are prohibited in all factories without exception
options.D: The Inspector may permit such operations without any rules

e: Section 87 of the Factories Act, 1948 empowers the State Government to make rules declaring an operation dangerous and prohibiting or regulating employment of women, adolescents or children in it.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, a worker who apprehends imminent danger to his life or health in a factory may:

options.A: Only stop work and leave the factory without informing anyone
options.B: Approach the Inspector only after the accident has occurred
options.C: Bring the apprehension to the notice of the occupier, agent or manager of the factory, and also to the notice of the Inspector, directly or through his representative in the Safety Committee
options.D: File a case in the civil court as the only remedy

e: Section 41H of the Factories Act, 1948 allows a worker apprehending imminent danger to his life or health to bring it to the notice of the occupier, agent or manager and also of the Inspector, directly or through his Safety Committee representative.

q: Under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, all wages payable to persons employed in a factory shall be paid:

options.A: In current coin or currency notes, or by cheque, or by crediting the wages in the bank account of the employee
options.B: In kind, in the form of articles produced in the factory
options.C: Partly in cash and partly in the form of goods, at the option of the employer
options.D: Only in cash, payment by cheque or bank credit being prohibited

e: Section 11 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 requires wages to be paid in current coin or currency notes, or by cheque, or by crediting the wages in the employee's bank account.

q: Under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, which of the following is an authorised deduction from the wages of an employed person?

options.A: A deduction for damage to the employer's property not attributable to the worker
options.B: A deduction by way of fine beyond the limit prescribed under the Act
options.C: A deduction for absence from duty for a period longer than the period of absence
options.D: A deduction for house accommodation supplied by the employer, and for such amenities and services (other than tools and raw materials) supplied by the employer, not exceeding the value of the accommodation, amenities or services

e: Section 7 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 authorises deduction for house accommodation and for amenities and services supplied by the employer, not exceeding their value; the other options exceed authorised limits.

q: Under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, deductions from the wages of an employed person for payments to co-operative societies, or for the premium on a scheme of insurance, shall:

options.A: Be made by the employer at his discretion, without reference to the worker
options.B: Not be made unless the deduction has been authorised in writing by the person employed
options.C: Be made only with the oral permission of the chargeman
options.D: Never be made under any circumstances

e: Section 7 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 permits deduction for payments to co-operative societies or insurance premia only when authorised in writing by the person employed.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, suitable arrangements for sitting are required to be provided and maintained in a factory:

options.A: Only in the office rooms of the factory
options.B: Only for workers who have completed twenty years of service
options.C: For all workers obliged to work in a standing position, so that they may take advantage of any opportunities for rest which may occur in the course of their work
options.D: Only in factories employing women workers

e: Section 47 of the Factories Act, 1948 requires suitable sitting arrangements for all workers obliged to work standing, so they may use opportunities for rest occurring in the course of work.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, a worker shall not enter any chamber, tank, vat, pit, pipe, flue or other confined space in a factory in which dangerous fumes are likely to be present, unless:

options.A: He merely holds his breath while inside the space
options.B: He enters during the lunch interval of the factory
options.C: Another worker stands outside the space, this being the only requirement
options.D: The space has been duly certified in writing by a competent person as safe, that is, free from dangerous fumes and fit for a person to enter, or he is provided with the prescribed means of egress and protection

e: Section 36 of the Factories Act, 1948 bars entry into a confined space with likely dangerous fumes unless it is certified in writing by a competent person as safe, or the prescribed means of egress and protection are provided.

q: Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 'lock-out' means:

options.A: The temporary closing of a place of employment, or the suspension of work, or the refusal by an employer to continue to employ any number of persons employed by him
options.B: The total or partial cessation of work by a body of persons employed in an industry
options.C: The retrenchment of surplus staff of an establishment
options.D: The closure of an establishment on a weekly holiday

e: Section 2(l) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 defines lock-out as the temporary closing of a place of employment, or suspension of work, or refusal by an employer to continue to employ any number of persons employed by him.

q: 'Tapping', as carried out in a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Cutting internal threads in a drilled hole by means of a tap
options.B: Cutting external threads on a rod by means of a die
options.C: Enlarging a drilled hole by means of a reamer
options.D: Producing a flat surface by means of a file

e: Tapping is the operation of cutting internal threads in a drilled hole by means of a tap; cutting external threads with a die is threading or dieing, not tapping.

q: 'Broaching', as carried out in a workshop, is a machining operation in which:

options.A: The workpiece is rotated and a single-point tool is fed against it
options.B: Metal is removed by a rotating abrasive wheel
options.C: Material is removed by pushing or pulling a long multi-tooth cutting tool, the broach, past or through the workpiece, each successive tooth cutting slightly deeper
options.D: A hole is produced by the spark erosion of the metal

e: Broaching removes material by pushing or pulling a long multi-tooth tool, the broach, past or through the workpiece, each successive tooth cutting slightly deeper than the previous one.

q: 'Hobbing', as carried out in a workshop, is the process of:

options.A: Finishing the bore of a cylinder by abrasive stones
options.B: Cutting gear teeth on a blank by means of a rotating worm-shaped cutter, the hob, which generates the teeth as it meshes with the rotating blank
options.C: Rolling threads on a bolt blank between flat dies
options.D: Producing a knurled surface on a cylindrical job

e: Hobbing cuts gear teeth on a blank with a rotating worm-shaped cutter, the hob, which generates the teeth as it meshes with the rotating blank.

q: 'Tumbling' (barrel finishing), as carried out in a workshop, is a process in which:

options.A: Castings are shaken out of their moulds by a vibrating grid
options.B: Molten metal is stirred in the cupola to mix the charge
options.C: Small parts are heated in a rotating furnace for hardening
options.D: Small components are cleaned and deburred by being rotated in a barrel or drum together with abrasives or other media

e: Tumbling or barrel finishing cleans and deburrs small components by rotating them in a barrel or drum together with abrasives or other media.

q: 'Pickling' of metal components in a workshop is the process of:

options.A: Removing scale, rust and oxides from the surface of the metal by immersion in a dilute acid bath, the cleaned surface being thereafter washed and neutralised
options.B: Preserving the components by coating them with grease
options.C: Colouring the components by heating them in oil
options.D: Testing the hardness of the components by pressing a ball into them

e: Pickling removes scale, rust and oxides from a metal surface by immersion in a dilute acid bath, after which the cleaned surface is washed and neutralised.

q: In resistance welding, as carried out in a workshop, the parts are joined:

options.A: By melting a filler rod in an oxy-acetylene flame
options.B: By hammering the heated parts together in the smithy
options.C: By the heat generated by the resistance of the parts themselves to the passage of a heavy electric current through them, the parts being held together under pressure
options.D: By dipping the parts in a bath of molten solder

e: In resistance welding the joint is made by heat generated by the resistance of the parts themselves to a heavy electric current passed through them, the parts being held together under pressure.

q: A carburising (reducing) flame in oxy-acetylene welding in a workshop is a flame in which:

options.A: There is an excess of oxygen over acetylene
options.B: There is an excess of acetylene over oxygen, the flame showing an intermediate acetylene feather between the inner cone and the outer envelope
options.C: Oxygen and acetylene are present in exactly equal proportions
options.D: No acetylene is used at all

e: A carburising or reducing flame has excess acetylene over oxygen and shows an intermediate acetylene feather between the inner cone and the outer envelope of the flame.

q: In machining operations in a workshop, the 'feed' of a cutting tool refers to:

options.A: The speed at which the tool or the work rotates, in revolutions per minute
options.B: The depth to which the tool cuts into the work
options.C: The total length of the cut made by the tool
options.D: The distance the tool advances into or along the work for each revolution or stroke of the work or the tool

e: In machining, feed is the distance the tool advances into or along the work for each revolution or stroke of the work or tool, distinct from speed and depth of cut.

q: A dividing head, as used with a milling machine in a workshop, is an attachment employed for:

options.A: Dividing the circumference of a workpiece into any required number of equal parts, as for cutting gear teeth, flutes or splines, and for rotating the work by a precise amount
options.B: Holding long shafts steady during turning on a lathe
options.C: Measuring the angles of a finished component
options.D: Dividing metal sheets into equal strips for shearing

e: A dividing head on a milling machine divides the circumference of a workpiece into any required number of equal parts, as for gear teeth, flutes or splines, rotating the work by a precise amount.

q: Patterns for foundry castings are dimensioned with the help of a 'shrink rule' (contraction rule), which is:

options.A: An ordinary standard rule used for all measurements in the pattern shop
options.B: A rule used for measuring the moulding sand in the foundry
options.C: A rule graduated longer than the standard measure by the contraction allowance of the metal concerned, so that the pattern is automatically made oversize to allow for the shrinkage of the casting on cooling
options.D: A rule used only for measuring finished castings after fettling

e: A shrink or contraction rule is graduated longer than standard by the metal's contraction allowance, so the pattern is automatically made oversize to allow for shrinkage of the casting on cooling.

q: The 'distortion allowance' (camber allowance) provided on a foundry pattern in a workshop is given because:

options.A: The casting expands uniformly in all directions on cooling
options.B: Certain castings distort or warp on cooling, and the pattern is therefore intentionally made distorted in the opposite direction so that the casting assumes the correct shape
options.C: The moulding sand shrinks as it dries in the mould
options.D: The pattern itself is expected to be damaged during moulding

e: Distortion or camber allowance is given because certain castings distort or warp on cooling; the pattern is made distorted in the opposite direction so the casting assumes the correct shape.

q: A 'straight edge', as used in the fitting and inspection sections of a workshop, is an instrument used for:

options.A: Marking centre lines on round bars
options.B: Measuring the thickness of thin sheets and wires
options.C: Cutting straight lines on sheet metal
options.D: Testing the straightness or flatness of surfaces, the gap between its true edge and the surface being judged by light or by feeler gauges

e: A straight edge is used to test straightness or flatness of surfaces, the gap between its true edge and the surface being judged by light or by feeler gauges.

q: On a zonal railway, the workshops of the railway function under the Mechanical Department, which at the headquarters of the railway is headed by:

options.A: The Principal Chief Mechanical Engineer
options.B: The Principal Chief Engineer (Civil)
options.C: The Principal Chief Operations Manager
options.D: The Principal Chief Commercial Manager

e: On a zonal railway the workshops function under the Mechanical Department, which at railway headquarters is headed by the Principal Chief Mechanical Engineer.

q: Promotion of artisan staff in railway workshops from one skilled grade to a higher skilled grade is made:

options.A: On the basis of seniority alone, without any test of skill
options.B: By nomination of the shop incharge
options.C: Through trade tests, designed to test the practical skill and trade knowledge of the artisan for the higher grade
options.D: By a written examination in general knowledge only

e: Promotion of artisan staff from one skilled grade to a higher skilled grade is through trade tests designed to test the practical skill and trade knowledge of the artisan for the higher grade.

q: Under the Factories Act, 1948, the expression 'manufacturing process' includes, among other things:

options.A: The running of trains on the open line of a railway
options.B: Generating, transforming or transmitting power, and preserving or storing any article in a cold storage
options.C: The sale of articles in a railway refreshment room
options.D: The booking of passengers and parcels at a station

e: Section 2(k) of the Factories Act, 1948 includes in manufacturing process generating, transforming or transmitting power and preserving or storing any article in cold storage.

q: The outturn of a workshop job has been fully transferred to its final head, yet the folio of the job in the Workshop General Register still shows a balance. The correct position is that:

options.A: The balance may be left as it is, since the job is physically complete
options.B: No balance should remain against a fully transferred job, and the residue must be investigated and cleared under proper orders
options.C: The balance should be transferred to the oldest running job of the shop
options.D: The balance should be written off to the Pension Fund at the year end

e: No balance should remain in a job folio after its outturn is fully transferred to the final head; any residue must be investigated and cleared under proper orders.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A worker's job card records the time spent by him on the individual jobs on which he was engaged.
2. The gate attendance card of a workshop records the time of entry and exit of the worker, that is, his attendance.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: A worker's job card records time spent by him on the individual jobs he was engaged on, while the gate attendance card records his time of entry and exit, that is, his attendance. Hence both.

q: Designs and drawings are prepared in the drawing office of a workshop exclusively for one particular manufacture job and for no other work. The cost of preparing those designs and drawings is:

options.A: Charged to that particular job
options.B: Spread over all the jobs of the workshop as general on-cost
options.C: Charged to the stores depot
options.D: Borne by the pattern shop as its on-cost

e: Cost of designs and drawings prepared exclusively for one particular manufacture job is charged to that particular job, since it is incurred solely for that job.

q: Cranes and traversers of a workshop move material internally for the shops generally, and their working serves the workshop as a whole rather than any one job. The cost of such internal transport is treated as:

options.A: A direct charge on the job whose material was moved last
options.B: Shop on-cost of the erecting shop alone
options.C: A deduction from the material cost of jobs
options.D: General on-cost of the workshop

e: Cost of cranes and traversers doing internal transport for the shops generally serves the workshop as a whole and is therefore treated as general on-cost of the workshop.

q: A chargeman proposes to start overtime working in his shop on his own authority to clear a backlog of work. The correct position is that overtime work in a workshop is undertaken:

options.A: Only with the prior sanction of the competent authority
options.B: At the discretion of the chargeman, sanction being obtained afterwards if convenient
options.C: Only by casual labour engaged for the purpose
options.D: Only on the weekly holiday of the workshop

e: Overtime working in a workshop is undertaken only with the prior sanction of the competent authority; a chargeman cannot start overtime on his own authority.

q: An apprentice engaged in a railway workshop under the Apprentices Act, 1961 claims incentive bonus on the same footing as a direct worker of the shop. The claim is not tenable because such an apprentice is:

options.A: A regular employee of the workshop on a time scale of pay
options.B: A trainee who is paid a stipend during training and is not treated as a worker of the workshop
options.C: Casual labour engaged on daily wages
options.D: An essential indirect worker of the shop

e: An apprentice under the Apprentices Act, 1961 is a trainee paid a stipend during training and is not treated as a worker of the workshop, so he cannot claim incentive bonus as a direct worker.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Intermediate Overhaul (IOH) of rolling stock from its Periodic Overhaul (POH)?

options.A: IOH is carried out only after the stock meets with an accident
options.B: IOH is heavier than POH and is carried out only in production units
options.C: IOH is a lighter overhaul carried out between two Periodic Overhauls to keep the stock in serviceable condition
options.D: IOH and POH are two names for one and the same overhaul

e: Intermediate Overhaul is a lighter overhaul carried out between two Periodic Overhauls to keep the rolling stock in serviceable condition, whereas Periodic Overhaul is the heavy prescribed overhaul.

q: Mid-Life Rehabilitation (MLR) of a coach in a workshop is distinguished from a mere repainting of the coach in that MLR is aimed at:

options.A: Converting the coach into a parcel van
options.B: Reducing the tare weight of the coach
options.C: Changing the livery of the coach only
options.D: Extending the service life of the coach by heavy mid-life repairs and renewal of fittings

e: Mid-Life Rehabilitation extends the service life of a coach by heavy mid-life repairs and renewal of fittings, and is therefore much more than a mere repainting or livery change.

q: Machines in a workshop are not lubricated at random, but according to a prepared lubrication schedule laid down for each machine. Observing such a schedule mainly helps to:

options.A: Ensure that every machine is lubricated regularly at the proper intervals, reducing wear and breakdowns
options.B: Increase the incentive bonus of the machine operators
options.C: Reduce the number of entries in the Plant Register
options.D: Avoid the need for any repair of the machines thereafter

e: A prepared lubrication schedule ensures every machine is lubricated regularly at proper intervals with the correct lubricant, reducing wear and breakdowns.

q: A workshop proposes to absorb the on-cost of all its shops on jobs at one single blanket rate for the workshop as a whole. The objection to a blanket rate, as compared with separate rates for each shop, is that:

options.A: A blanket rate is not permitted to be revised at any time
options.B: The indirect expenses of different shops differ widely, so a blanket rate would overcharge some jobs and undercharge others
options.C: A blanket rate can be applied only to revenue jobs
options.D: Separate shop rates cannot be worked out from the shop accounts

e: A single blanket on-cost rate is objectionable because indirect expenses of different shops differ widely, so it would overcharge jobs of low on-cost shops and undercharge jobs of high on-cost shops.

q: In work study in a workshop, method study is undertaken before work measurement mainly in order to:

options.A: Fix the wages payable to the staff of the shop
options.B: Distribute the on-cost of the shop over its jobs
options.C: Examine and improve the method of doing the work, so that time is thereafter measured for the standardised method
options.D: Compute the bonus earned by a gang of workers

e: In work study, method study is done before work measurement to examine and improve the method of doing the work, so that time is thereafter measured for the standardised method.

q: Work sampling is employed in a workshop, in place of continuous observation, mainly in order to determine:

options.A: The chemical composition of the metals used on jobs
options.B: The price of stores items in the price ledger
options.C: The periodicity of overhaul of rolling stock
options.D: The proportion of time spent by men and machines on various activities, including the extent of idleness

e: Work sampling, in place of continuous observation, determines the proportion of time spent by men and machines on various activities, including the extent of idleness.

q: In work measurement, the predetermined motion time system abbreviated as MTM stands for:

options.A: Methods-Time Measurement
options.B: Machine Time Measurement
options.C: Material Transfer Method
options.D: Measured Task Method

e: In work measurement, MTM stands for Methods-Time Measurement, a predetermined motion time system based on standard times for basic human motions.

q: Under Taylor's differential piece-rate system of wage payment, a worker is paid:

options.A: A guaranteed time wage having no relation to his output
options.B: At a higher piece rate if he attains or exceeds the standard output, and at a lower piece rate if he falls short of it
options.C: Time wages plus one-half of the value of the time saved by him
options.D: A bonus worked out as a proportion of his time taken

e: Under Taylor's differential piece-rate system, a worker attaining or exceeding standard output is paid at a higher piece rate, and one falling short of it at a lower piece rate.

q: In the fixing of allowed times in a workshop, a 'loose rate' means an allowed time which is:

options.A: Shorter than the time properly required for the job
options.B: Built up entirely from standard data
options.C: More liberal, that is longer, than the time properly required for the job
options.D: Fixed only for non-repetitive jobs

e: In fixing allowed times, a loose rate means an allowed time more liberal, that is longer, than the time properly required for the job; the opposite, a tight rate, is shorter.

q: A worker under the incentive scheme spends part of his time rectifying his own defective work which was rejected on inspection. For that rectification time, he:

options.A: Earns bonus at double the normal rate
options.B: Is treated as on leave without pay
options.C: Has the time charged to the next job taken up by him
options.D: Earns no bonus, bonus being payable only on accepted good work

e: A worker earns no bonus for time spent rectifying his own defective work rejected on inspection, bonus being payable only on accepted good work.

q: It is noticed in the Workshop Accounts Office that labour and material have been booked to a wrong work order. The correction of the booking is effected by:

options.A: Transfer entries debiting the correct work order and crediting the wrong one, passed under proper approval
options.B: Erasing the original entry in the shop records
options.C: Booking the amount again to the correct work order, leaving the wrong booking untouched
options.D: Writing off the amount to shop on-cost

e: Booking of labour or material to a wrong work order is corrected by transfer entries debiting the correct work order and crediting the wrong one, passed under proper approval.

q: For components manufactured regularly in a workshop, standard costs are prescribed mainly so that:

options.A: Actual job costs need never be compiled for such components
options.B: The actual cost of each batch or job can be compared with the standard cost and the variations analysed for cost control
options.C: No on-cost need be charged on such components
options.D: The components can be sold to the trade at the standard cost

e: Standard costs for regularly manufactured components let the actual cost of each batch or job be compared with the standard and variations analysed for cost control.

q: The period for which a rolling stock unit remains detained in a workshop for its overhaul is watched closely mainly because:

options.A: The workshop charges rent for every day of detention of the unit
options.B: Detention earns incentive bonus for the shop staff
options.C: Prolonged detention reduces the effective availability of rolling stock for traffic
options.D: The unit is transferred to the stores depot after one month of detention

e: Detention of a rolling stock unit in a workshop for overhaul is watched because prolonged detention reduces the effective availability of rolling stock for traffic.

q: Before the job cards and tally sheets of a shop are rendered to the Workshop Accounts Office, the time booked by the workers on them is certified by:

options.A: The stores depot attached to the workshop
options.B: The Production Control Organisation
options.C: The cash office of the workshop
options.D: The shop supervision, that is, the chargeman or foreman of the shop concerned

e: Before job cards and tally sheets are rendered to the Workshop Accounts Office, the time booked on them is certified by the shop supervision, that is, the chargeman or foreman of the shop.

q: The incentive bonus payable to workshop staff for a period is, before payment:

options.A: Computed by the executive on the basis of the outturn and the allowed times, and checked by the Workshop Accounts Office
options.B: Computed by the stores depot on the basis of material issued
options.C: Paid at a flat rate to all staff, irrespective of outturn
options.D: Computed by the Railway Audit office after the annual accounts are closed

e: Incentive bonus for a period is computed by the executive from outturn and allowed times and is checked by the Workshop Accounts Office before payment is made.

q: The Productivity Linked Bonus paid to railway employees is distinguished from the incentive bonus of a workshop in that the Productivity Linked Bonus is:

options.A: Earned only by the workers of one particular shop
options.B: A railway-wide payment linked to the productivity of the Railways as a whole, and not to the outturn of an individual worker or shop
options.C: Computed on the time saved by each individual worker
options.D: Paid only in production units manufacturing locomotives

e: Productivity Linked Bonus is a railway-wide payment linked to the productivity of the Railways as a whole, unlike workshop incentive bonus which depends on an individual worker's or shop's outturn.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The codal life of rolling stock is its prescribed economic service life, on the completion of which the stock normally becomes due for condemnation and replacement.
2. Rolling stock which has completed its codal life is condemned automatically, without any examination of its condition.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: Both 1 and 2
options.B: 2 only
options.C: 1 only
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Codal life is the prescribed economic service life after which stock normally becomes due for condemnation and replacement, but completion of codal life does not condemn it automatically without examination. Hence 1 only.

q: Before a rolling stock unit is taken up for Periodic Overhaul in a workshop, the usual first step is to:

options.A: Dismantle the unit completely
options.B: Paint the unit in the new livery
options.C: Transfer the unit to the stores depot
options.D: Examine the unit and assess the repairs required, so that the scope of the overhaul is decided

e: Before a unit is taken up for Periodic Overhaul, it is first examined and the repairs required assessed, so that the scope of the overhaul is decided before dismantling begins.

q: After manufacture or heavy repair in the boiler shop of a workshop, a boiler is subjected to a hydraulic (hydrostatic) test before it is passed for use. The test is carried out mainly in order to:

options.A: Prove the soundness of the boiler and detect any leakage under pressure
options.B: Clean the inside of the boiler of scale and rust
options.C: Paint the boiler under pressure
options.D: Fix the allowed time for the boiler shop staff

e: A boiler after manufacture or heavy repair is hydraulically tested mainly to prove its soundness and detect any leakage under pressure before it is passed for use.

q: The expenditure on testing and trial runs of a newly manufactured locomotive or coach, incurred before its acceptance, is treated as:

options.A: A charge to the shop on-cost of the workshop as a whole
options.B: A part of the cost of manufacture of that unit, charged to its job
options.C: A revenue expense of the open line
options.D: A loss to be written off to revenue

e: Expenditure on testing and trial runs of a newly manufactured locomotive or coach before acceptance forms part of the cost of manufacture of that unit and is charged to its job.

q: For non-repetitive jobs in a workshop, where continuous stop-watch study is impracticable, allowed times are fixed by:

options.A: Asking each worker to name his own time for the job
options.B: Adopting the allowed time of an unrelated job
options.C: Analytical estimating, building up the time from synthetic or standard data and the judgement of trained estimators
options.D: Dispensing with allowed times for such jobs altogether

e: For non-repetitive jobs where stop-watch study is impracticable, allowed times are fixed by analytical estimating, building up time from synthetic or standard data and trained estimators' judgement.

q: Patterns for foundry castings are made slightly larger than the finished casting required. This is done in order to provide for:

options.A: The thickness of paint to be applied on the casting
options.B: Errors in weighment of the metal charge
options.C: Expansion of the moulding sand when heated
options.D: Shrinkage, that is contraction, of the metal as it cools and solidifies

e: Foundry patterns are made slightly larger than the finished casting to provide for shrinkage, that is contraction, of the metal as it cools and solidifies.

q: In a foundry, the cores used for forming the hollow portions of castings are prepared in:

options.A: The core shop, that is, the core-making section
options.B: The pattern shop
options.C: The fettling shop
options.D: The machine shop

e: Cores used for forming the hollow portions of castings are prepared in the core shop or core-making section of the foundry, not in the pattern, fettling or machine shop.

q: Processes such as hardening, tempering and annealing of steel components in a workshop are carried out in the:

options.A: Smithy
options.B: Heat treatment shop
options.C: Foundry
options.D: Wheel shop

e: Processes such as hardening, tempering and annealing of steel components are heat treatment processes and are carried out in the heat treatment shop of the workshop.
